toc.title: The water is your autonomic state
The water moves, not the light
Why Stoic practice can feel so hard
The water carries every wave before it
Where Stoicism and the nervous system meet

blocks.p: This one brings in another passion of mine, outside of but connected to mental health and the nervous system: philosophy, particularly Stoic philosophy. The metaphor I'll discuss might help illustrate topics you're already familiar with if you know my work. And if you're into Stoicism, you'll be familiar with the concepts already, but I want to challenge how you think about them, and maybe what you do with that information.

I was reading through the Discourses by Epictetus. I have a little morning ritual where I read a bit of it, and this quote in particular really hit me. I read it a few times, and I thought it was worth discussing. Here it is:

q: Such as is a dish of water, such is the soul. Such as is the ray of light which falls on the water, such are the appearances. When the water is moved, the ray also seems to be moved, yet it is not moved.

blocks.p: So what is Epictetus actually saying? There are three main pieces of this I'd like to focus on. The quote continues, but we have enough to work with right here. Those three pieces are water, light, and appearances.

The first element of the metaphor is water. Water is your soul. For the Stoics, the soul is not some immaterial thing floating around within your physical body. It's the ground of your consciousness: your capacity to perceive, to reason, to choose. In their language, it's the hegemonikon, the ruling faculty. It's what makes you uniquely you, and it's what makes humans different and unique from other animals.

The second piece of the metaphor is the light, or reality itself. The external world: events, other people, the way things actually are, independent of how you're experiencing them or what you think of them. Events unfold, people act, the world keeps on spinning. The fundamental nature of reality, the order that governs how things work, remains constant and objective. That's the light.

The third element of the metaphor is the appearances. I didn't really find a great singular definition of appearances. They all deal with the same realm. So I'll use my own understanding based on my readings, and for those familiar with Stoicism, I'm going to leave out the piece about assenting to appearances.

In Stoic terms, appearances are your immediate impressions of reality: from the initial sensory input, to a cognition about it, a thing in the brain, to an emotion about it. Appearances are the rapid and conscious experiences that take place between input and behavior, that you don't control, but that you can notice.

As an example, let's say you've ordered a coffee from your favorite cafe. You've been waiting all day to get out of work, and you finally have the chance to have your desired beverage. You take the first sip, anticipating its assured deliciousness, but by golly, it's the wrong one.

Your consciousness receives the sensory input of the wrong coffee. Maybe it's a plain black coffee, which is what I prefer, and you were expecting a sugary one. Which is okay every now and then, but plain black is the way to go, typically.

So the sensory input hits, and then you probably have a physical reaction, like disgust. You've been waiting all day, so you also feel the emotion of frustration. The words "Darn it!" pop into your brain. All of these are appearances: the taste, the disgust reaction, the emotion, and the words in your brain.
How you use this information to inform your behavior, and whether or not the appearances spiral into other emotions, is another matter.

blocks.h: The water is your autonomic state

blocks.p: Let's bring this back to the original metaphor: "Such as is a dish of water, such is the soul."

Soul for Epictetus meant your capacity to consciously choose. But your capacity to choose is not exactly something you choose. You don't choose your capacity to choose, right? Something else influences it, and no, it's not your mindset. It's not your will.

In physiological terms, your capacity to choose is determined by the state of your autonomic nervous system. If your system is in a state of defense, your capacity to consciously choose a Stoically virtuous behavior, for example, is significantly diminished. If you're in a state of flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze, you're less likely to choose a virtuous behavior than if your body were in a state of safety, where you have more flexibility to notice an appearance, pause and hold it, use logic to process it, and then choose a virtuous behavior.

The autonomic states I listed, flight, fight, freeze, and shutdown, aren't just emotions or a way of thinking. They're physiological states of the body, linked to the sympathetic and parasympathetic branches of the autonomic nervous system.

So when Epictetus says, "Such as is a dish of water, such is the soul," we can reword it: such as is a dish of water, such is the autonomic state. The dish of water is the metaphor for the autonomic state. Ideally, the dish of water is calm and still. Ideally, the autonomic state is calm and still, or at least well regulated and flexible. Not rigid, not frozen in fear, but capable of meeting reality with openness.

The second part of the metaphor concerns light and appearances: "Such as is the ray of light which falls on the water, such are the appearances." The ray of light is objective reality. That's easy enough.

Appearances are the conscious initial experiences of objective reality. They're a result of reality. In the Stoic view, they follow sensory input from reality. But we need to pause here and understand how reality and those conscious initial experiences interact. We need to spend more time on the connection between the light and the water.

Appearances, the initial impressions of reality, don't exist on their own. They're triggered by events in the external world. That's true. But appearances come through the body's autonomic state. The autonomic state acts as a filter through which sensory experiences pass. So it's not just sensory input, then conscious experience of that input. It's deeper than that. It's sensory input into the autonomic state, which filters the input, then produces the conscious output.

The body's autonomic state could be a result of the present moment, sure. But usually, especially for us humans, it's also a result of the past. The past context of our lives shapes our nervous systems, limiting or expanding our potential responses to the internal appearances triggered by external reality.

Person A might have a baseline of safety in their system, so they live with more patience and can make a Stoic, virtuous, logical decision. When person A receives the wrong coffee, they'll take it as an opportunity to calmly respond and resolve the situation. They'll notice any initial appearances of frustration, maybe contain them, process how they want to respond, thank fortune for providing the opportunity for growth, and then resolve the situation.

But person B might have more shutdown chronically in their system. Their autonomic state is primed for collapsing and feigning death, playing dead. So in our coffee example, they're more likely to shrink away and not say anything, and they'll use the coffee incident to secretly shame themselves for being too small or too weak.

I gave the example of two different people, but person A, who reacts more Stoically, could easily be person B on a bad day. Or maybe they used to be person B years ago, and were able to get unstuck and become person A. Or maybe person A becomes person B after an extreme life event brings them into that shutdown state.

Our nervous systems are elastic. They adapt based on the needs of survival. Your body's ability to self-regulate now is not the same as it was in the past, and it will likely be different in the future. And sadly, our nervous systems can get stuck in a defensive state of flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze.

Typically, our bodies are never truly at a calm baseline. We're constantly bombarded by stimuli from reality, plus our past affects us. Plus we have bills to pay, and work is tomorrow, and the kids won't get along, and we have judgments about all these things.
So we can reword this part of the metaphor: such as reality affects the autonomic state and is filtered through the autonomic state, such are conscious experiences.

blocks.h: The water moves, not the light

blocks.p: Epictetus continues: "When the water is moved, the ray also seems to be moved, yet it is not moved."

The light, reality, doesn't change. The external world doesn't change. The water changes, and because the water changes, the appearances change, even though the light remains constant. One's autonomic state is always changing. The water is never really quite still. It's possible to have that stillness, yes, but typically we're not in a state of stillness day to day. So every input that comes in through your senses passes through your autonomic state, which always has some level of defense in it, different from person to person, of course.

So what do we do about this? The light moving on the surface of the water is not caused by the light itself. It's caused by the movement of the water. Does the external world have issues? Of course it does. Major ones, even. But there are probably things in your daily life that dysregulate you, like getting the wrong coffee, or somebody at work not doing their job, that don't need that level of dysregulation.

blocks.h: Why Stoic practice can feel so hard

blocks.p: Stoics train to notice the appearances and to pause before reacting. Something happens. They have a bodily reaction to it, an appearance. They catch and contain it. They reflect on what to do with it using cognitive tools, and then they enact the logical response.

I think that when people first encounter Stoic practice, they often treat it as a technique or a mindset, as if pure willpower and logic can override what's happening in their nervous system. If this sounds difficult to you, it's because it is. It requires lots of restraint, and lots of noticing what's happening within you in the present moment.

Stoicism is primarily known as a cognitive philosophy, even as a form of psychology. It blends easily into cognitive behavioral therapy. But it demands an incredible amount of present moment mindfulness. So this is great if you can be this present-moment aware, have this much restraint, think logically through an appearance, and enact a logically chosen behavior, which of course is in alignment with nature. But there might be an easier way. Or maybe a deeper way, a more sustainable way.

blocks.h: The water carries every wave before it

blocks.p: The problem with how many people approach Stoic practice is that they view the moment of tasting the coffee as a single point in time. And yes, it is a single point in time. But they view that one moment as isolated from all the previous ones. They view your capacity to react as if it came from a baseline that resets with every moment, as if you're starting fresh. That's not how it works.

This current moment is obviously influenced by the previous ones, as reflected in your autonomic state. Your state's not random. It's the normal and expected result of your life context. It's shaped by what happened last week, what happened last year, what happened in your childhood.

The water doesn't exactly reset. It carries the memory of all the waves before it. The external world is filtered through the autonomic state, and not just the present autonomic state, but the compilation of previous moments leading to the current one.

The solution, then, is not to control the outside world. It's not to white-knuckle your way through life with iron discipline, either. It's to calm your autonomic state. Once you do that, the appearances caused by reality will be much less intense. You'll be better able to notice them, to let them be, to think through them, and to make a better decision.

blocks.h: Where Stoicism and the nervous system meet

blocks.p: Understanding your autonomic state and studying Stoicism have a really nice intersection. They're not mutually exclusive at all, I don't think. Understanding your state sheds light on potential frustrations you have with your Stoic practices, if you're trying to implement these very cognitive practices. It explains why some days the practices flow, and other days it feels like you're fighting against yourself.
Stoicism does not deny emotions. Stoicism doesn't teach you how to repress your emotions, either. That's not my reading of it. Your emotions are real, just as the external world is real.

But Stoicism does encourage you to focus on what you can control. You can't change your nervous system state through wishing or willing. I'm sure you've tried. But you can connect with your nervous system state in the present moment. You can spend time with it. You can become more curious about your inner world and your responses to it.

You can't control what happens. You can't control other people. You can't control external events. But you can, over time, with practice, learn to settle your own internal state, so that you can perceive clearly and respond more wisely. This is the heart of Stoic freedom: not freedom from the world, but freedom in how you meet the world.

In my one-on-one therapy and coaching work with clients, I always save problem solving and homework assignments until the end of the session. Why? Because at the beginning and in the middle of the session, we're reviewing previous homework and processing what went well and what didn't over the past week or so.

But we're also intentionally and mindfully connecting with the present moment, with the experience of safety in the present moment. After we connect with the present and with safety, we intentionally connect with defensive activation. But not by itself. We connect with defensive activation and balance it with safety.

The present moment connection can lead us to balancing defense. Once the body is in a balanced state, problem solving becomes much easier: more clear, more compassionate and empathetic, for the self and for others. This is the practice of settling the water.
"How the heck do I do that in my real daily life?"
It's harder outside of one-on-one work, for sure. But there are a few simple things you can start now that don't require much time or effort, and are pretty darn realistic for anybody.

Number one: practice simple mindfulness every day. Notice what your senses are telling you. I don't mean count objects in the room to decrease your anxiety. I mean use one of your senses intentionally, with as much focus as you can. When you drink your tea, really taste it. On the next sip, really feel the warmth through your body. Just focus on one thing at a time.

Simple mindfulness practices bring a bit of safety into your autonomic state as you connect with the present moment. In other words, you're focusing on your experience of external reality, but choosing to do so in small doses when you have the most capacity for it, not when you're spiraling in anxiety.

Number two: after you practice simple mindfulness, notice how that one intentional act affects your next breath. Don't control your breath. There's no need to. Your body knows how to breathe, so let it, and stop getting in the way. Just mindfully connect with the natural in and out rhythm of your next breath.
Number three: after you practice simple mindfulness, and after you connect with your breath, honestly acknowledge the pains you're carrying around with you.
So sip the tea. Notice its warmth. Then check your in and out breath. Then acknowledge your lingering sadness, maybe. And then repeat.

We're not trying to force ourselves to be calm or virtuous. We're not trying to pretend things don't matter. We're doing the slower, deeper work of building the capacity to meet reality as it actually is, without denying the truths of our inner pains.

You and I can make progress on that together, and so can the next person who hears this. Imagine how much could change if each of us embraced our potential to steady our own water. And imagine what would happen if we worked together on steadying each other's waters, in parallel.
